newsitem.title: UK: UK set for PSBR undershoot even without tax rise.
newsitem.headline: UK set for PSBR undershoot even without tax rise.

text.p: Britain is on course to undershoot official forecasts for the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) whether or not there are tax rises at the July 2 budget, analysts say.
Thursday's upward revision to the projected profile of the budget deficit has not dented the healthy picture of the public purse.

"It doesn't change what is a very dramatic downward trend in the PSBR. The economic news we've had since November will completely swamp the impact of these assumptions," J.P. Morgan economist David Mackie said.
"Even if the July 2 budget didn't happen, this year's PSBR would be revised down by maybe up to five billion pounds."

The new Labour government has changed the assumptions underlying Treasury forecasts and, had these been in place at the November budget, the PSBR prediction for fiscal 1997-98 would have been 19.7 million stg not 19.2 million.

Further out, the upward revisions go as high as seven billion stg. The new assumptions -- which the Treasury stressed were not actual forecasts -- won the approval of the National Audit Office, an independent body responsible only to parliament.
The figures sparked newspaper headlines about a "black hole" in the public finances which Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown might have to fill with tax rises.
However, analysts say the Treasury exercise in changing the public finance assumptions was purely hypothetical and does not justify higher tax.
"The report looks like something that Brown might look to, to try and excuse extra taxation, but the finances really aren't that bad," Morgan Stanley economist Mark Miller said.
"I don't think we'll get a big net fiscal tightening in the budget. We're probably looking at a maximum of 2.0 billion pounds."
The figures have not caused economists to revise upward their forecasts for the PSBR.
"The change in the assumptions really hasn't made any difference," said HSBC UK economist Dharshini David.
"We're still looking for a PSBR of 12.0 billion pounds this year and five billion pounds next, in line with a fiscal tightening of four or five billion," she said.

J.P. Morgan's Mackie is also going for a PSBR of 12.0 billion stg this year but sees the deficit at 8.0 billion in 1998-99, compared with the November budget projection of 12.0 billion, which would have been 15.3 billion on the new basis.
BZW analyst Kevin Adams argues that Brown may well revise the forecast for the current year deficit down to 12.0 billion stg but argues the out-turn is likely to be closer to 16.5 billion.
"The spending numbers have been very good so far but we think they will start to overrun later in the year," he said.

Brown has pledged to stick to the previous, Conservative administration's pledge to increase spending by just 2.0 percent over the next two years but analysts argue that the figures will be very hard to achieve.

Both the education and the health service are hungry for funds and such stringent spending control has never before been achieved. Even so, the public finances are heading back towards balance. Adams, who is forecasting a fiscal tightening in July of just 2.5 billion stg, sees the PSBR in 1998-99 dipping to 14.5 billion pounds. Morgan Stanley's Miller is more relaxed, looking for a PSBR of 15.0 billion stg this year, plummeting to 7.0 billion stg next as the economic growth rate gathers pace, boosting government revenue from taxes and at the same time cutting its benefit bill.
